contentBlocks.heading: The Primary Years Programme, and what comes after it
contentBlocks.body:
The Primary Years Programme is the IB's framework for children aged 3 to 12. Learning is organised around six transdisciplinary themes: Who we are; Where we are in place and time; How we express ourselves; How the world works; How we organize ourselves; and Sharing the planet. Children explore these themes through units of inquiry, and the ten attributes of the IB learner profile run through all of it. Students complete the PYP exhibition in the final year. There are no external examinations.

To parents raised on textbooks and unit tests, this can feel vague. Your child may come home talking about how a market works, and you may wonder what was actually learnt. Reading, writing and maths still matter at every age, and the class teacher can tell you where they sit in the current unit, which is exactly what an IB Primary Years tutor needs to know. A child who flourishes in discussion but is shaky on number facts needs different help from one who knows their tables and freezes at an open question.

Leaving the PYP needs planning a year ahead, not a summer ahead. A child continuing into the Middle Years Programme enters a five-year programme (MYP 1 to 5, roughly ages 11 to 16) across eight subject groups, where every subject is assessed against four criteria, A to D, each scored 0 to 8. Children who settle quickly tend to be the ones who can already explain their thinking in writing and organise a longer piece of work. A tutor in the final PYP year can make those habits deliberate.

Moving to a Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) or Indian Certificate of Secondary Education (ICSE) school is a different adjustment. Families often describe it as more textbook content, more written tests and a second language expected at a set level, so the gaps to watch are usually Hindi, formal grammar and fast written calculation.
items: Six transdisciplinary themes, explored through units of inquiry, for children aged 3 to 12
No external examinations in the PYP; the exhibition comes in the final year
MYP: five years, eight subject groups, criteria A to D scored 0 to 8
Moving to CBSE or ICSE: ask for the entry-class books and syllabus early

contentBlocks.heading: Reading, maths and units of inquiry: where a tutor helps
contentBlocks.body:
Reading is where most primary IB home tuition should start, because almost everything in a unit of inquiry depends on it. A child who decodes slowly spends all their energy on the words and has nothing left for the ideas. Listen for guessing at longer words from the first letter, losing the place on the page, reading aloud flatly without noticing a question mark, and being unable to retell a page in their own words. An IB PYP English tutor works on these with books the child chooses, short daily reading targets and plenty of talk about the story.

Maths at this age is about number sense more than speed. A child with secure foundations splits 47 into 40 and 7 without thinking, sees that 6 times 4 and 4 times 6 are the same, and estimates before calculating. A child without them struggles quietly as soon as a unit asks them to collect data, measure something or handle money. A good IB PYP tutor in Gurgaon reaches for coins, a measuring tape and the kitchen scale before a workbook, and asks 'how did you get that?' far more often than 'what is the answer?'

Here is what an inquiry-friendly session can look like. Suppose a Grade 4 class is working under Sharing the planet, in a unit about water. There is no worksheet on the water cycle. Instead, the child reads a short newspaper piece about water tankers in a Gurgaon summer, underlines two unfamiliar words and works out their meaning from the sentence. Then they time a running tap for 30 seconds, measure what collects in a jug, and scale that up to a week of brushing teeth with the tap left on. The last ten minutes go on one question the child wants to take back to class. It is still reading, measurement and multiplication, but it feels like the child's own investigation, which is what PYP inquiry learning support should feel like.
items: Reading: decoding, fluency aloud, retelling a page, and working out vocabulary from context
Maths: place value, multiplication facts, estimation and measurement with real objects
Writing: two or three sentences explaining how the child reached an answer
Units of inquiry: one real question each session, carried back into class
Final PYP year: note-taking, interviewing an adult and organising findings clearly

contentBlocks.body:

Along Golf Course Road, in DLF Phase 5, DLF Phase 1, Sector 42, Sector 43, Sector 53, Sector 54, Ardee City and Wazirabad, a late-afternoon home slot is realistic when the tutor lives on the same stretch, subject to availability. Otherwise ten minutes of a young child's best attention disappear in the lobby.

Sector 47, Sector 48, Sector 49, Sector 50, Nirvana Country, South City 2, Rosewood City, Uppal Southend and Badshahpur all feed towards Vatika Chowk, where evening traffic can stretch a short trip. Families in Central Park Resorts, Orchid Petals, Vatika City, Malibu Towne, Vipul Greens and The Close tend to do better with a tutor already on that side, or with weekend morning lessons. In the DLF Phases 2 to 4, MG Road and Cyber City belt, taking in DLF Phase 2, DLF Phase 3, DLF Phase 4, Sikanderpur, Chakkarpur, Sector 24, Sector 27 and Sector 28, distances look small but office traffic builds early, so parents in DLF Beverly Park, Heritage City, DLF Hamilton Court, DLF Regency Park, DLF Richmond Park and Ambience Caitriona usually find an earlier slot easier to keep.

contentBlocks.heading: School calendars in Gurgaon and the PYP exhibition year
contentBlocks.body:
Parents often search for tutors alongside school names such as Pathways World School, Lancers International School, Scottish High International School, GD Goenka World School, The Shri Ram School, Aravali, and Heritage Xperiential Learning School. Those names are local context only. This page does not describe what any of them teach, and IB Gram is an independent platform, not affiliated with any school named here, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge International Education or Pearson Edexcel.

Across international schools in Gurgaon, the pressure points for primary families are about rhythm more than exams. A new unit of inquiry can change what your child reads and talks about almost overnight. Reports and parent conferences may lean on written comments rather than marks, which some parents find harder to act on. Long summer and winter breaks give a slow reader time to catch up, but they also let fragile number facts fade. And a family trip around Diwali or the December holidays can leave a child a week behind in the middle of a unit.

The final PYP year adds the exhibition, and it deserves its own plan. Your school decides how it runs, including whether children work in groups, who mentors them and how findings are shared, so ask the PYP coordinator early in the year. PYP exhibition help from a tutor is legitimate when it builds the child's own capacity: narrowing a broad interest into a question they can actually investigate, practising how to interview an adult, reading a source at the right level, planning backwards from the school's dates, and rehearsing a presentation until it sounds like them.

It stops being help when an adult chooses the question, writes the text, designs the display or finds every source. Teachers generally notice, and the child misses the point of the whole exercise. One rule keeps everyone honest: the tutor may ask any question, but the child's hand holds the pen.
items: Ask the PYP coordinator how the exhibition runs at your school this year
Use long holidays for daily reading, not a stack of revision worksheets
Keep unit newsletters so the tutor knows what the class is exploring
Exhibition rule: the tutor asks questions; the child chooses, writes and presents

contentBlocks.heading: Home, online or hybrid: what suits a PYP learner in Gurgaon?
contentBlocks.body:
For most children under eight, home lessons work best, because reading aloud, counting real objects and watching a child's face all need a tutor in the room. Online lessons start to work from about Grade 3 or 4, once a child can sit, listen and manage a shared screen with a little help. Hybrid suits the exhibition year and families in outer sectors.

For a PYP child, the trade-off is plain. Home tutoring gives the closest attention and the easiest use of books, blocks and the kitchen scale, but it depends on the tutor's travel, needs an adult at home and can be hard to arrange in some sectors. Online tutoring widens the choice of tutors with IB experience and removes travel, but a young child's attention drifts quickly on a screen and an adult usually needs to stay nearby. Hybrid, meaning mostly online with a home visit every week or two, keeps a specialist involved while giving the child regular face-to-face contact, though it takes more planning to keep both halves connected.

Home lessons suit this age for reasons that have little to do with convenience. A tutor sitting beside a seven-year-old can hear the tiny hesitation before a word, see a finger slide back along a line, and push a pile of coins across the table when carrying tens will not land. Young children learn a great deal by handling things and moving around, which a screen cannot offer. So for primary IB home tuition focused on reading and early number, an IB PYP home tutor in Gurugram, physically at the table, is worth the logistics.

But online is sometimes the better call. A confident ten-year-old who needs help planning exhibition research or writing clear explanations may do well with a PYP online tutor, especially where the nearest suitable home tutor lives across the city, as can happen in New Gurgaon. Keep the laptop in a shared room rather than a bedroom.
items: Home: best for ages 3 to 8, reading aloud and hands-on maths
Online: workable from about Grade 3 or 4, with an adult nearby
Hybrid: an online specialist plus regular home visits, useful in the exhibition year
New Gurgaon families: consider hybrid when no suitable specialist lives nearby
Any mode: ask for a one-line note on what your child did

contentBlocks.heading: Checking a home tutor who will sit with a young child
contentBlocks.body:
A tutor for a primary-age child needs a different kind of scrutiny from a tutor for a teenager. You are letting someone into your home, or onto your child's screen, for regular time with a person who cannot always tell you when something feels wrong. IB Gram shortlists tutors whose profiles are verified. That is a necessary first filter, not a judgement on whether this particular person can hold a six-year-old's attention. Only you can judge that, and the trial session is where you do it.

Ask questions that reveal how the tutor thinks about young children. How would they help a Grade 2 child who guesses at words? What would they do if your child refused to read on a bad day? How would they use the unit of inquiry the class is on? An IB PYP tutor in Gurgaon with real experience of the programme talks about the child first and the material second. Be wary of anyone who offers a printed workbook for every week of the term before meeting your child.

During the trial, watch rather than hover. Notice whether the tutor lets silence sit while your child thinks, whether they praise effort in specific words, and whether your child talks more by the end than at the start. Confirm the tutor's identity at the gate on the first visit, keep lessons in a common room, and make sure a parent or known caregiver is at home throughout.

Afterwards, ask your child one thing: would they like this person to come back? Six-year-olds are blunt, and the answer is usually useful. Then set a few boundaries in writing. Messages go to a parent's phone, never the child's; photos of work come to you and nowhere else; and lessons do not move to a tutor's home or a park without your agreement.
items: Confirm the tutor's identity at the society gate on the very first visit
Ask how they would help a Grade 2 child who guesses at words
Keep lessons in a common room with a parent or caregiver at home
All messages go to a parent's phone, never directly to the child

contentBlocks.heading: Does your child need a PYP tutor at all?
contentBlocks.body:
Often, no. A PYP child needs a tutor when a specific foundation is slipping and has not recovered after a term of school support: reading well behind classmates, number facts that still need fingers in Grade 4, or a child who has turned anxious about school. If school simply feels unstructured to you, talk to the teacher first.

The signs worth acting on are specific and persistent. Your Grade 3 child avoids reading aloud and invents excuses to skip the bedtime book. Written work in the unit folder is far shorter than the talk they can produce. They cannot tell you whether 38 is nearer 30 or 40. Or the child says 'I'm bad at maths' and clearly means it. Any one of these, lasting more than a few weeks, is reason to find an IB PYP tutor in Gurgaon for targeted help, usually with reading or number.

Signs that a tutor is not needed matter just as much. A child who reads happily but spells creatively at six is usually fine. So is a Grade 1 child who cannot yet sit through a worksheet, or a final-year child whose exhibition plans look chaotic in the early weeks. Wanting a head start on the MYP or an Olympiad is not, by itself, a reason to give a nine-year-old two more hours of structured work a week. Free play, sleep and reading for pleasure do more for most children at this age than extra tuition does.

Some worries need someone other than a tutor. If your child still reverses letters well past the early years, struggles to follow spoken instructions, or cannot settle in any setting, speak to the school counsellor or learning support team about an assessment first. And if the real issue is a poor fit with a class or a teacher, extra lessons at home will not fix it.
items: Needs help: reading avoidance and halting reading aloud that lasts several weeks
Needs help: number facts still counted on fingers by Grade 4
Probably fine: creative spelling at six, or messy early exhibition planning
Not a reason on its own: a head start on the MYP or Olympiads
Ask the school about an assessment for persistent letter reversal or attention worries

contentBlocks.heading: What should progress look like after a term of PYP tuition?
contentBlocks.body:
After a term of regular sessions, progress should show in behaviour before it shows in school reports: a child who reads aloud with less fuss, attempts a maths problem before asking for help, and explains how they reached an answer. Reading level and number fluency usually move more slowly, over one or two terms.

In the first three or four weeks, look for small things. Your child stops hiding when the tutor arrives. The bedtime book comes out without a negotiation. Written explanations grow from one line to three. If none of that has happened by the end of the first month, ask the tutor what they are seeing, and if the answer is vague, ask IB Gram for a different match rather than waiting out a whole term.

Because the PYP has no external examinations, there is no score to chase, and parents sometimes reach for worksheets or tests to prove the tuition is working. Resist that. Better evidence is a short running record: the book your child is reading now compared with the one in June, a maths explanation from week one beside one from week ten, and the class teacher's comments across two reports. For an older PYP child, add one more marker: can they plan a small investigation, such as a survey of how classmates travel to school, without an adult deciding each step?

Some limits deserve plain words. No tutor can guarantee a particular reading level, a report comment or a smooth move into the MYP. A tutor cannot replace ten minutes of reading with a parent each evening either, and a child worn out by school, a football class and an abacus class will not learn much in a fourth commitment. If progress stalls, the fix is sometimes fewer activities, not a better tutor.
items: Weeks one to four: less resistance and longer written explanations
One to two terms: reading level and number fluency begin to move
No progress after a month: ask the tutor, then ask for a different match
No tutor can guarantee a reading level, a report comment or a smooth MYP move

contentBlocks.heading: How should PYP tuition in Gurgaon begin for your child?
contentBlocks.body:
Start small: two sessions a week, 30 to 40 minutes each for children aged 5 to 7 and around 45 minutes for most children aged 8 to 11, at a time of day when your child is still fresh. Before the first session, share the current unit of inquiry, a recent report and one book your child enjoys.

Attention is the real limit at this age, not the syllabus. A six-year-old concentrates in short bursts, so a good 35-minute session changes activity every ten minutes or so, moving from reading to a maths game to a short chat about the unit. A ten-year-old can hold one task for longer, and an occasional 60-minute planning session in the exhibition year is reasonable. Two short sessions usually beat one long weekly session, because young children forget a lot between Saturdays. And a child who has just stepped off a long school bus ride will learn little, whatever the tutor does.

A good first session is mostly listening. The tutor hears your child read aloud, plays a short number game to find where understanding is secure, and asks what the class is exploring. It should not open with a written diagnostic test, which tells a nervous seven-year-old that this is another exam. At the end, expect five minutes with you covering what the tutor noticed, what they would work on first, and one thing to try at home that week, such as reading a recipe together and doubling the quantities.

When you send the query, include your child's grade, the worry in one sentence, the free afternoons or weekend mornings, and your sector or society, whether that is DLF Phase 3, Sector 49 or Sector 85. Review the plan after four weeks, and drop to one session a week once the gap closes. Tuition at this age should have an end point in sight.
items: Ages 5 to 7: roughly 30 to 40 minutes, changing activity every ten minutes
Ages 8 to 11: around 45 minutes, with longer planning sessions in the exhibition year
First session: reading aloud, a number game and a talk about the unit
Review after four weeks and reduce sessions once the gap has closed

faqs.question: Is a tutor worth paying for when the PYP has no exams?
faqs.answer: It is worth it when there is a specific gap to close, and rarely worth it as general enrichment. Without exams, the return shows up later, when a child reaches the MYP able to read a dense text and explain their reasoning in writing. But paying for extra worksheets for a child who is already coping well buys very little. If you cannot name the problem in one sentence, speak to the class teacher first.

faqs.question: Is home tuition better than a PYP online tutor for a six-year-old?
faqs.answer: For most six-year-olds, yes, although a few do learn well online. Early reading and counting depend on a tutor catching small hesitations and handing over real objects, and a screen makes both harder. If you try online, keep sessions to around 25 to 30 minutes, make them lively, and have an adult sit nearby to handle the device. Judge it after three sessions rather than one. From about Grade 3, online becomes far more practical.

faqs.question: What if my child and the tutor do not get along?
faqs.answer: Ask for a different match; it is a normal request, and you can make it whenever the fit is wrong. With young children a poor fit usually shows quickly: tears before sessions, refusing to come to the table, or a tutor who talks over the child. Allow two or three sessions first, because some children are shy with any new adult. Then tell IB Gram what did not work, whether pace, tone or approach, so the next suggestion takes it into account.

faqs.question: There has been no improvement after a month. What should we do?
faqs.answer: Ask the tutor to show you something your child could not do in week one and can do now, then change one specific thing. If the tutor cannot point to anything, check the basics. Is the session at a time when your child is exhausted? Does the work connect to the current unit? Is anyone reading with your child between sessions? If those are fine and still nothing has moved, ask IB Gram for a different match rather than adding more hours.

faqs.question: How can a tutor give PYP exhibition help without doing the work?
faqs.answer: A tutor helps by asking questions and teaching skills, while your child chooses the topic, writes the text and builds the display. That means turning 'I like animals' into a question about stray dogs in your society, practising an interview with a vet or a resident welfare association member, showing how to take notes from a website in their own words, and rehearsing the presentation. Check the school's guidance on outside help with the PYP coordinator, and keep the tutor's role visible to the teacher.

faqs.question: My child is moving from the PYP to a CBSE or ICSE school. How do we prepare?
faqs.answer: Start a few months ahead by getting the new school's books for the entry class and closing the specific gaps they reveal. A tutor can work through the first chapters of each book with your child, build a steady homework routine and practise written calculation. If Hindi or another second language is new to your child, give it the most time, because it is the hardest part to rush. Do not try to cover the whole year in advance; that tends to produce anxiety, not readiness.

faqs.question: Will a home tutor travel to Sector 84 or Sector 89 on weekday evenings?
faqs.answer: It depends on tutor availability, and in New Gurgaon a weekend morning or an online slot is often easier to arrange than a weekday evening. A suitable PYP tutor may live some distance from Sector 84, Sector 89 or societies such as Godrej Air, and evening traffic can stretch even a short trip. For a young child, a tutor arriving late into a tired evening is a poor trade. Share your exact sector and free slots when you send a query, so location is part of the match.

faqs.question: Should a Grade 3 tutor be giving my child worksheets every session?
faqs.answer: No; a few worksheets are fine, but they should not fill every session. A good IB Grade 3 tutor in Gurgaon teaches multiplication by building arrays with buttons and asking the child to explain them, and improves reading through talk about real books. contentBlocks.heading: From first message to a Maths IA mentor shortlist in Gurgaon
contentBlocks.body:
A request for IB Maths IA help in Gurgaon is a different request from weekly Maths lessons, and the matching reflects that. A student who is behind on calculus needs content teaching. One who is three weeks from the school's draft date needs someone who can read a proposed aim, see that the mathematics is too thin for the course, and ask the question that lets the student see it too.

So the first conversation is specific. IB Gram asks whether your child takes AA or AI, at SL or HL, in DP1 or DP2. We ask where the exploration stands: no topic yet, a topic the teacher has queried, data collected but no model, or a draft already returned with comments. The school's internal dates matter too, because a mentor who is free on Saturdays is little use if the draft is due on a Thursday. Then come location and schedule: your sector or society, the evenings genuinely free after school timings and activities, and whether home, online or hybrid lessons suit you.

What comes back is a shortlist of tutors whose profiles are verified and whose experience fits that brief, subject to availability for your child's level and schedule. A demo or trial session can be arranged before you commit. In that session, watch one thing closely: does the tutor ask your child to explain their own working, or explain it for them? An IB Maths IA tutor in Gurgaon who fills every silence with explanation may be a fine teacher, but an exploration needs a mentor who can wait.

If the fit turns out to be wrong, you can ask for a different match. With an IA, say so early. Changing mentor a fortnight before submission costs far more than changing in the first month, because a new mentor has to learn the topic and data from scratch.

2. IB Gram asks where the exploration stands, from no topic to a returned draft.

contentBlocks.heading: Does the exploration change between AA and AI, or SL and HL?
contentBlocks.body:
The task stays the same; the mathematics expected of the student does not. AA and AI students at SL and HL all write an exploration of 12-20 pages, marked out of 20 on the same five criteria and worth 20% of the final grade. The level of mathematics should follow from the course, and HL work is judged against a higher standard on criterion E, Use of mathematics.

That 20% carries real weight in the Diploma Programme. A DP student takes six subjects, each graded 1-7, and Theory of Knowledge (TOK) and the Extended Essay (EE) add up to 3 more points, so the maximum is 45; 24 points is the minimum for the diploma, subject to the IB's failing conditions. A fifth of the Maths grade rests on work produced over several weeks rather than in a timed exam, which is a real opportunity for a student who freezes in exam halls.

The course names are a fair guide. An exploration built on algebraic or analytical argument, such as generalising a pattern and proving it, often suits Analysis and Approaches students. Applications and Interpretation students are often better served by one built on real data and modelling, where the choice of model and the reading of results carry the weight. Neither is a rule. An IB Maths AA IA tutor should still push a data-led topic towards genuine analysis, and an IB Maths AI IA tutor should still expect precise argument rather than a spreadsheet printout.

Maths IA HL help often starts from one worry, that the mathematics is not enough. HL runs on 240 recommended teaching hours against 150 at SL, and a topic that suits SL can look thin once criterion E is judged at the higher standard. The opposite mistake happens too: an impressive-sounding topic the student cannot explain. Before the topic is fixed, ask the Maths teacher what depth of mathematics they expect.
items: Same task for AA and AI, at SL and HL: 12-20 pages, out of 20, worth 20%.
HL work is judged against a higher standard on criterion E, Use of mathematics.
AA explorations often suit proof and generalisation; AI explorations often suit data and modelling.
Ask the Maths teacher what depth of mathematics suits the course before fixing a topic.

contentBlocks.heading: IB Maths IA criteria A to E, and what moves each mark
contentBlocks.body:
The five IB Maths IA criteria add up to 20 marks: A Presentation (4), B Mathematical communication (4), C Personal engagement (3), D Reflection (3) and E Use of mathematics (6). Criterion E carries the most weight. But A and B are where marks slip away most easily, and they are also the quickest to recover.

Presentation marks follow structure. State the aim clearly on the first page, let each section follow from it, and end with a conclusion that answers it. Cut anything that does not serve the aim, including a page of biography about a famous mathematician. Mathematical communication is about language: define variables before using them, keep notation consistent, label axes with units, and never leave calculator shorthand such as x^2 or 3.2E-4 in the text. Put each graph or table where it is discussed, not in an appendix.

Personal engagement is the most misunderstood criterion, and it is not a hobby story. A paragraph about loving cricket earns nothing on its own. The mark moves when the student's thinking shows in the mathematics itself: they collected the data, asked a question the textbook did not, or tried a second model when the first fitted badly. Reflection works in a similar way. A closing list of limitations is thin. Stronger reflection runs through the exploration: why this model rather than another, what an assumption does to the result, whether a surprising number makes sense, and what the finding means for the original aim.

Use of mathematics, worth 6, is where the substance is judged. Fewer techniques done properly beat a long list done loosely, and every step should be there because the aim needs it. Your child should be able to explain any line without notes. For HL, the criterion is judged against a higher standard, so depth, not length, separates an ordinary E from a strong one.
items: A Presentation (4): a clear aim early, logical sections, a conclusion that answers it.
B Mathematical communication (4): defined variables, consistent notation, labelled axes, no calculator shorthand.
C Personal engagement (3): the student's own questions and decisions visible in the mathematics.
D Reflection (3): comments on method, assumptions and meaning throughout, not just at the end.
E Use of mathematics (6): fewer techniques, done correctly, explained, at the course's level.

Every school sets its own internal deadlines for the IB internal assessment in Maths, and the date that matters most is the draft. We never assume a school's programme or deadlines from its name; we ask the family, and suggest checking with the DP coordinator if they are unsure.

The pressure rarely comes from the Maths exploration alone. It tends to arrive alongside internal assessments in other subjects, Extended Essay work, TOK and university applications, all squeezed around long school days and bus routes. Exam sessions run in May and November; May is the session most Gurgaon IB schools use, and May results are released in early July. Coursework dates come from the school, so put each one in the family calendar the week it is published.

Picture a student who returns from the long summer break with data collected but no model, and with the EE and another subject's IA also waiting. The workable plan is to fix the aim and choose the model within two weeks, draft the sections that carry the most marks first, and leave the polish until after the teacher's comments. Starting the Maths write-up the weekend before the draft is due does not work, however capable the student.

contentBlocks.heading: Is an IB Maths IA tutor in Gurgaon better at home or online?
contentBlocks.body:
For most of the exploration, online works at least as well as home, because the work already lives on a screen: spreadsheets, graphing software and typed mathematics. Home sessions earn their place at the start, when a student is choosing a topic and thinks best aloud over rough paper. A hybrid plan, home for planning and online for reviews, suits many Gurgaon families.

Home tutoring suits a student who drifts when unsupervised, one who reasons best with pen and paper, and the first topic conversation, when the mentor needs to see the notebook, the half-formed questions and the data the student hopes to use. The costs are travel and flexibility. Evening traffic on Golf Course Extension Road or SPR can push a start time back, and an extra home slot is hard to add at short notice in the week before a draft.

An IB Maths IA online tutor can watch your child share a screen and run a regression in a spreadsheet, adjust a model in GeoGebra or Desmos, or step through a short Python simulation, while the student keeps control of the file. That last point matters for integrity: the student types, the tutor asks. Short online check-ins of 30 minutes also fit more easily around school timings when several deadlines land in the same fortnight.

Home, online or hybrid mentoring for a Maths IA comes down to one trade-off. Home tuition gives the best focus for topic choice and for students who need someone in the room, but it costs travel time and flexibility. Online gives the clearest view of software and data and the quickest short reviews, but a distracted student can drift off-camera. Hybrid pairs a home session for planning with online reviews near the draft date, and it works only if the family keeps both arrangements running.

contentBlocks.heading: Where does legitimate IA mentoring stop and ghostwriting start?
contentBlocks.body:
Mentoring stops at the student's words, choices and calculations. A tutor can teach the mathematics the exploration needs, question the student's reasoning and explain what each criterion looks for using other examples. A tutor must not choose the topic, write or rewrite any sentence, do the calculations, draw the graphs or correct the draft line by line. The work must be the student's own.

The grey areas need clarity. Helping a student test topic ideas they brought, by asking what mathematics each would need, is legitimate; the choice stays with the student. Pointing out that reflection is thin and asking about the model's main limitation is also fine, provided the student writes the answer. So is teaching curve fitting on a different dataset. The teacher can comment on one draft, so an outside mentor annotating that draft first blurs whose work the teacher is reading. Ask the Maths teacher how the school wants outside support declared, and follow that.

IB Gram shortlists tutors whose profiles are verified and whose experience matches the course and level. A verified profile is not a verdict on fit, so before an IB Maths exploration tutor starts, run your own checks in the demo. Ask directly what they will do with your child's draft. A good answer is specific: no typing in the document, no corrected version sent back, no calculations to copy. Be wary of anyone offering a finished topic, a sample exploration to adapt, or edits to make the work sound better.

Then check the basics. Has the tutor taught the course your child takes, AA or AI, at that level? Can they explain criterion E without reading from a sheet? Do they ask your child, early on, to explain the idea in their own words? A mentor who talks for most of the demo is teaching, which helps before exams but not with an IA.
items: Can do: teach needed mathematics, question reasoning, explain criteria through other examples.
Cannot do: choose the topic, write or edit text, calculate or plot for the student.
Walk away from offers of finished topics, sample explorations or polished rewrites.
Follow the school's rule on declaring outside support, and ask the teacher if unsure.

contentBlocks.heading: Which Maths IA topics work, and which ones usually fail?
contentBlocks.body:
A topic works when it gives the student real mathematics to do at the level of their course, and a reason to care about the answer. It fails when the mathematics has already been done by someone else, or when it sits beyond what the student can explain. Maths IA topic ideas help only when each is tested against those two conditions; a ready-made list rarely survives.

Three types of topic tend to hold up. The most dependable is modelling something the student can measure, such as a cup of chai cooling on the counter or a ball's flight filmed on a phone. Your child collects the data, chooses between models and explains where the model breaks down, which feeds criteria C, D and E at once. A statistical question about data the student understands also works, for example seasonal air-quality readings from a published source, provided the analysis goes beyond averages and bar charts to a method the student can justify. For many AA students, the third option is taking a known result further: generalising a pattern, proving it and testing where it stops holding.

Two types usually fail. The famous-topic essay, on the golden ratio in art or the history of pi, tends to describe mathematics other people did, leaving little room for criteria C and E. The borrowed-advanced topic fails the other way. A student lifts a model from a university website, perhaps on neural networks or option pricing, and cannot explain the steps. When the teacher asks a simple question about one line, the gap shows.

Data and technology decide feasibility as much as the idea does. Before committing, the student should know where every number will come from and which tool will handle it: a spreadsheet for regression, GeoGebra or Desmos for fitting curves, Python for simulation. Published data needs a cited source. And technology should do the arithmetic, not the thinking.
items: Works: modelling something the student can measure, such as cooling chai or a ball's flight.
Works: a statistical question about data the student understands and can source properly.
Works for many AA students: extending a known result, then proving the generalisation.
Usually fails: a famous-topic essay describing mathematics that other people already did.
Usually fails: an advanced model borrowed from elsewhere that the student cannot explain.

contentBlocks.heading: Topic to final submission: an IA timeline built around the draft date
contentBlocks.body:
Progress on an exploration is measured in decisions, not pages. The timeline below counts backwards from the school's draft date, which the Maths teacher or DP coordinator can confirm.

1. Eight to ten weeks before the draft date, the student lists three topic ideas and notes the mathematics and data source for each.
2. Around seven weeks before, the student chooses one topic and writes a one-paragraph aim, sharing it with the Maths teacher if the school invites that.
3. Five to six weeks before, data is collected or sourced and the student tries a first model or method on it.
4. Three to four weeks before, the core mathematics for criterion E is complete and the student can explain every step.
5. Two weeks before, every section is written, reflection runs throughout, and notation, graphs and the 12-20 page length are checked.
6. On the draft date, the complete draft goes to the teacher, whose comments guide the final version.
7. Before the school's final deadline, the student acts on each comment, rechecks all five criteria and submits the final exploration.

Healthy progress is easy to spot. After three weeks of mentoring, your child can state the aim in one sentence and say why the mathematics suits it. By the draft, they can talk through the model without the document open. Trouble looks different: the topic keeps changing, the data has not arrived, or sessions go on re-explaining the same method.

The limits deserve plain words. No tutor can guarantee a grade on the IA, and a mentor cannot mark the work in place of the teacher. Starting two weeks before the draft narrows what is possible: the topic largely stays, and the realistic aim becomes clearer communication and reflection. Some well-organised students with a clear topic and a responsive teacher need no mentor at all, or just one session to test the plan.
items: Three weeks before the draft, core mathematics is done and explainable without notes.
On draft day, every section is attempted, with reflection throughout, within 12-20 pages.
Warning sign: the topic is still changing five weeks before the draft.
No tutor can guarantee a grade, and no mentor replaces the teacher's comments.

contentBlocks.heading: Getting started with an IB Maths IA tutor in Gurgaon
contentBlocks.body:
Before the first session, gather what the school has already given your child. That usually means the course and level, the internal draft and final dates, any IA guidance sheet or criteria handout from the Maths teacher, and comments on a topic proposal if there were any. Add the student's own list of ideas, however rough, and any data already collected, in whatever form it exists. If the school has an academic integrity policy or a form for declaring outside help, bring that too, so the mentor works within it from the first session.

The first session is about the student, not the tutor. Expect the mentor to ask your child to explain each idea aloud, what mathematics it would use and where the data would come from. By the end, there should be a shortlist of one or two viable topics, a list of what the student must find out before choosing, and a date for the next session tied to the school calendar. If the topic is already fixed, the first session tests the aim and planned method against the IB Maths IA criteria instead.

For a DP2 student whose draft has already come back, the first session looks different. The tutor goes through the teacher's comments with the student, not the draft line by line, and helps turn each comment into a task the student will do alone. Nothing is rewritten in the session. At this stage, one well-run session is sometimes enough.

To begin, send a query or book a free consultation with IB Gram. Tell us the course, level, draft date, sector or society, free evenings and whether you want home tuition or online sessions. If you also want an IB Maths tutor in Gurgaon for weekly lessons once the IA is submitted, mention it at the start, because it changes who belongs on the shortlist.

Bring any IA guidance sheet, criteria handout or comments on a topic proposal.

faqs.question: Can an IB Maths IA tutor write or correct parts of my child's exploration?
faqs.answer: No, an IB Maths IA tutor in Gurgaon or anywhere else cannot write, rewrite or correct any part of the exploration, because the work must be the student's own. A tutor can teach the mathematics your child needs, ask questions that expose a weak step, and explain each criterion using a different example. Your child then makes every change in their own document. A tutor who offers to tidy up the draft or send back an edited file should not continue.

faqs.question: How many mentoring sessions does a Maths exploration usually need?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed number, because it depends on where your child starts. A student with a settled topic, data in hand and a clear method may need only a few focused sessions around the draft. A student starting with no topic usually benefits from a session every week or fortnight across the two months before the draft date, plus short check-ins near the end. Plan backwards from that date rather than committing to a fixed count upfront.

faqs.question: My child wants to write about the golden ratio. Should they change the topic?
faqs.answer: Probably not the whole idea, but it usually needs reshaping before it can carry enough mathematics. As a description of where the golden ratio appears, it leaves little room for personal engagement or use of mathematics. It becomes workable when your child asks a question their own mathematics can answer, such as measuring a set of objects and testing whether the ratio really appears. A mentor asks the questions; the student chooses the new direction.

faqs.question: Can the exploration use published data instead of data my child collects?

contentBlocks.heading: How does IB Gram find a TOK tutor for a Gurgaon student?
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram asks what your child needs in TOK, which deadlines are close, and where and when lessons can happen, then shortlists tutors whose verified profiles match those needs. A demo session can be arranged before you commit, and you can ask for a different match if the fit is wrong.

The questions go further than they would for a Maths request, because a TOK student's difficulty is rarely missing content. One DP2 student has an exhibition built around objects the teacher has queried. Another has chosen a prescribed title and produced 400 words of opinion with no counterclaim in sight. A DP1 student may not have started either assessment and simply finds the class discussions baffling. Each needs a different kind of tutor, and an IB TOK tutor in Gurgaon who is excellent at rescuing a deadline may be the wrong person for a DP1 student who needs slow, patient discussion.

We also ask which two optional themes the class is studying and whether a teacher has commented on a draft or an object shortlist, because a good outside tutor works with that feedback, never around it. Location and timing come last but still matter. A student in DLF Phase 4 with a free Saturday morning and a student in Sector 108 off the Dwarka Expressway who is free only after 8 pm on weekdays may be matched with different tutors, even when the TOK problem is identical. A tired student argues badly at 9 pm, whoever the tutor is.

Some families arrive asking for IB TOK coaching in a batch. The demo is where you find out whether one-to-one discussion suits your child better, and the test is simple: notice how much of the session your child spends talking. If the answer is very little, tell us. That is useful information, not a complaint.

contentBlocks.heading: How do TOK and EE points count towards the IB Diploma?
contentBlocks.body:
Theory of Knowledge (TOK) and the Extended Essay (EE) are each graded A to E, and the two letters combine for up to 3 diploma points on top of six subjects graded 1-7, for a maximum of 45. An E in either is a failing condition, so it matters even with high subject grades.

The Diploma Programme (DP) runs over two years, DP1 and DP2. Students take six subjects from six groups, three or four at Higher Level (HL) and the rest at Standard Level (SL). Alongside them sits the core: TOK, the EE and Creativity, Activity, Service (CAS), which must also be completed. The diploma needs at least 24 points, subject to the IB's failing conditions.

The TOK letter comes from two assessments. The exhibition is an Internal Assessment (IA): three objects linked to one of 35 IA prompts, up to 950 words, assessed at school and worth one third of the TOK grade. The essay answers one of six prescribed titles released for each exam session, runs to a maximum of 1,600 words, is externally assessed and carries the other two thirds. Both draw on one course: the core theme, knowledge and the knower; two of five optional themes; and five areas of knowledge, which are history, the human sciences, the natural sciences, mathematics and the arts.

TOK is rarely where a diploma is won, but it is one place where a diploma can be lost. A student close to the 24-point line gains real security from a solid TOK letter, and a student with strong subjects still cannot afford an E. The exact letter combinations are set out in a matrix, so ask the school's DP coordinator for the current version rather than trusting a table copied from a forum. And because the two letters are read together, a weak EE raises the stakes on TOK.
items: Exhibition: three objects, one of 35 IA prompts, up to 950 words, one third.
Essay: one of six prescribed titles per session, up to 1,600 words, two thirds.
TOK and EE are graded A to E, together worth up to 3 points.
An E in either TOK or the EE is a failing condition.
Areas of knowledge: history, human sciences, natural sciences, mathematics and the arts.

contentBlocks.heading: What is a TOK knowledge question, and where does the exhibition fit?
contentBlocks.body:
A knowledge question is a question about knowledge itself: how we know something, how far a method can be trusted, and who gets to decide. It is open and arguable, and no single fact settles it. The exhibition puts this into practice, with three objects linked to one of 35 IA prompts and explained in up to 950 words.

One worked example shows the difference. On a smoggy November evening, two air-quality apps show different readings for the same Sector 50 society. The opinion question is 'Which app is right?' Checking where each sensor sits settles it, and the thinking stops there. The knowledge question sits one level up: 'How far should we trust a measurement when we cannot see the method that produced it?' A claim: published, checkable methods earn trust because other people can test them. A counterclaim: most people act on the number on their screen without checking anything, and often that trust is reasonable. Good TOK knowledge questions help a student carry one situation into several areas of knowledge.

Students often start the exhibition in the wrong place, collecting three interesting objects and then hunting for a prompt that fits them all. It usually works better the other way round: choose the prompt, list possible objects from the student's own life, and keep only those with a specific context. Not 'a smartphone', but the phone on which a grandmother in Sector 27 first learned to check a forwarded message before sharing it. A specific object gives the explanation something to hold; a generic one pulls the student back into opinion.

TOK exhibition help from a tutor means questions, not answers. Why does this object belong with this prompt? Do the three objects show the prompt from different angles, or say the same thing three times? Is the link to the prompt stated, or only implied? The tutor never picks the objects or drafts the words, and because the exhibition is internally assessed at school, the TOK teacher's guidance on object choice comes first.
items: A knowledge question asks how we know, not what we know.
Opinion: 'Which app is right?' Knowledge question: 'How far should we trust unseen methods?'
Exhibition order that usually works: the prompt first, then three specific objects.
The tutor questions each link to the prompt; the student chooses and writes everything.

contentBlocks.heading: Gurgaon corridors and what they mean for TOK home tuition
contentBlocks.body:

DLF Phases 2 to 4, MG Road and Cyber City. Homes in DLF Phase 2, DLF Phase 3 and DLF Phase 4, and in Sikanderpur, Chakkarpur and Sectors 24, 27 and 28, sit close together, so one tutor can often serve several societies. The catch is weekday evenings, when MG Road and the roads around Cyber City slow down and a short trip can stretch. Gated societies such as DLF Beverly Park, Heritage City, DLF Hamilton Court, DLF Regency Park, DLF Richmond Park and Ambience Caitriona usually log visitors at the gate, so register a regular home tutor once rather than fielding a security call every week. A workable pattern here: a longer weekend home session for essay planning, and a short weekday check-in online.

A tutor from across the city meets the Vatika Chowk and Badshahpur bottlenecks just as a DP student gets home. contentBlocks.heading: TOK deadlines and teacher expectations at Gurgaon schools
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram is an independent platform and is not affiliated with any school shown on this page, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge International Education or Pearson Edexcel. What follows is the general pattern at international schools in Gurgaon, not any one school's policy; the TOK teacher and DP coordinator hold the real dates.

Six prescribed titles are released for each exam session, and most Gurgaon IB schools use the May session, so a May candidate writes on one of those six. May results are released in early July. Inside that frame, each school sets its own internal steps for the essay, often a title choice, a plan, a draft the teacher comments on and a final version, along with its own deadline for the exhibition. Ask for those dates at the start of DP1. A family that first hears them from a class WhatsApp group in the week they fall is already behind.

The squeeze is predictable. At many schools, TOK milestones can land close to subject IA drafts, Extended Essay work and mock preparation, and TOK is the task students push back because it has no formula to revise. Picture a DP2 student in DLF Phase 3 with a Physics IA write-up, an EE reflection and a TOK essay plan all due inside one fortnight. That is often when families call. It is later than ideal, though still early enough to build a proper plan.

Teachers also expect TOK language. A plan full of 'I think' and 'in my opinion' will keep coming back with the same comment about a missing knowledge question. Outside help should use the school's terms and follow the teacher's feedback. If a teacher has said an object is too generic or a title has been misread, that comment becomes the opening agenda of the next session.
items: Ask the TOK teacher for internal exhibition and essay deadlines early in DP1.
Six prescribed titles are released for each exam session; students write on one.
Most Gurgaon IB schools use the May session; May results come in early July.
Expect possible overlap between TOK milestones, subject IA drafts, EE work and mocks.
Bring the teacher's written comments; they set the next session's agenda.

contentBlocks.heading: Home, online or hybrid: which works for TOK in Gurgaon?
contentBlocks.body:
Online TOK tutoring suits weekly discussion and feedback on plans, home tuition helps students who argue more freely face to face, and hybrid gives a family both. The trade-off is plain: home lessons cost travel time on weekday evenings in Gurgaon, while online depends on a student who keeps the camera on and actually talks.

TOK suits discussion because the course is about arguments, and arguments get better under pressure. A student's first response to a title is nearly always a position. The tutor's job is to push back: offer the counterclaim, ask for an example from a different area of knowledge, ask what evidence would change the student's mind. Hearing a claim challenged aloud, and having to defend it on the spot, is usually what turns a paragraph of opinion into an argument. Written comments alone rarely do that.

An IB TOK online tutor can run that discussion well if the session is set up deliberately. The tutor keeps a shared document open with the title or prompt at the top and a two-column table of claims and counterclaims underneath. The student speaks first, and the tutor types only keywords, so the student is thinking rather than dictating. Near the end, the student restates the strongest counterclaim in their own words, then writes the paragraph after the call, alone.

A home tutor earns their place when a student goes quiet on screen, or when an essay plan is easier to build with index cards moved around a dining table. In DLF Phase 3 or Sector 49 that is realistic with a nearby tutor. In Sector 106 on the Dwarka Expressway, it may mean a long evening journey, so online is usually more reliable. Hybrid, online on weekdays and a home session on a weekend before a deadline, is often the practical compromise.
items: Home: suits quiet students and card-based planning, but costs weekday evening travel.
Online: suits weekly discussion and plan feedback; needs the camera on and a student who talks.
Hybrid: weekday sessions online, a weekend home session before exhibition or essay deadlines.
Online sessions build a claims-and-counterclaims table live as the student talks.
The student drafts paragraphs alone after the session, never during the call.

contentBlocks.heading: How to check an IB TOK tutor in Gurgaon before lessons start
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram shortlists only tutors whose profiles are verified and match the TOK need. What verification cannot show you is how a tutor handles a sixteen-year-old's weak argument at 7 pm on a Tuesday, and that is what your own checks are for.

Start with a two-minute test in the demo or on the call before it. Give the tutor an ordinary opinion question, such as whether a particular news channel is biased, and ask them to turn it into a knowledge question. A strong TOK tutor does this easily and explains why the new version is arguable. A weak one produces something that still has a factual answer. Then ask what they do when a student asks them to write the introduction. The only acceptable answer is some version of no, followed by what they would do instead. Ask which areas of knowledge they draw examples from comfortably, too. A tutor with a science degree may lean heavily on the natural sciences, which is fine if your child's title needs that and a problem if it needs the arts or history.

Some warning signs are easy to spot: a promise of an A, an offer of 'model essays' on the current prescribed titles, a fixed template that forces every essay into one shape, or a tutor who talks through most of the demo. Any of these should end the conversation. The first two also create an academic integrity problem with the school, a far worse outcome than a weak TOK grade.

In the demo itself, watch who does the talking. If your child spoke for less than half the session, the tutor was lecturing, and TOK does not improve by lecture. Ask your child afterwards whether they felt free to disagree with the tutor. That answer tells you more than any profile.
items: Ask the tutor to turn an opinion question into a knowledge question on the spot.
Ask what they do when a student requests a written introduction.
Walk away from grade promises or 'model essays' on current prescribed titles.
During the demo, your child should talk more than the tutor.

contentBlocks.heading: How should a student plan the TOK essay on a prescribed title?
contentBlocks.body:
A student should plan the TOK essay by turning the prescribed title into the knowledge question it is really asking, choosing areas of knowledge that suit it, building a claim and counterclaim for each with a specific real-life example, and settling on a qualified conclusion before writing any prose. Planning should take longer than drafting.

The essay carries two thirds of the TOK grade, which is why planning deserves most of the tutoring time. The commonest weakness in early plans is not the writing. It is a student answering the topic instead of the title: writing everything they know about climate science when the title is really asking how disagreement shapes what counts as knowledge. Families looking for TOK essay help in Gurgaon often arrive at exactly this point, with a draft that is fluent and beside the point.

Claims, counterclaims and examples need precise meanings. A claim is a reasoned position on the knowledge question within one area of knowledge. A counterclaim is not simply the opposite opinion; it is the strongest reason the claim might be limited or wrong. Carry the air-quality situation into the natural sciences: the claim is that open, checkable methods justify trust, and the counterclaim is that people reasonably act on a reading, closing windows or skipping a morning walk, without understanding the method at all. Real-life examples should be specific enough to check, something named, dated or located, not 'scientists in the past'. Good TOK essay structure depends on this, because the vague example is where most plans quietly fall apart.

Old TOK prescribed titles help a student practise the whole process before the real list arrives, so the first attempt at unpacking a title is not the one that counts. The division of labour stays fixed throughout. The tutor questions the plan and the argument, much as the school's TOK teacher would. The student writes every sentence.
items: 1. Read your session's six prescribed titles and rewrite each as a knowledge question.
2. Choose one title, define its key terms and note what it assumes.
3. Pick areas of knowledge that suit the title and draft one claim for each.
4. Write the strongest counterclaim to each claim, with a specific, checkable real-life example.
5. Settle a qualified conclusion and map paragraphs against the 1,600-word limit.
6. Draft alone, then bring the plan and draft back for questioning, not rewriting.

contentBlocks.heading: What progress should TOK tutoring show, and by when?
contentBlocks.body:
Within three or four sessions, a student should usually be turning their own opinions into knowledge questions without prompting, and within about six weeks they should be able to argue against their own claim with a specific example. The TOK letter depends on the final exhibition and essay, so no tutor can guarantee a grade.

TOK progress has no worksheet score, so listen for the language changing at home, from 'that's just wrong' to 'it depends on who is measuring and how'. Look at the plans, too. A week-one plan is usually a list of topics; a week-six plan should line up claims, counterclaims and examples against the title. A student who once avoided class discussion and now volunteers a counterclaim is progressing too, even before any draft improves. And the teacher's comments on a draft should shift from a missing knowledge question towards depth and choice of examples.

The limits are worth stating plainly. A tutor cannot move a school's internal deadline. Nor can a tutor rescue an exhibition three days before it is due by rethinking the objects from scratch; at that stage the realistic job is strengthening the explanations the student already has. A student who skips the thinking between sessions will not improve simply because sessions happen. And starting in the final weeks before an essay deadline narrows the work to repairing one plan instead of building the habit of thinking in knowledge questions.

Some students do not need a TOK tutor at all. A student who enjoys class discussion, gets clear feedback and has a plan the teacher is happy with may need nothing more than a parent who asks about the title over dinner. If that sounds like your child, say so on the consultation call. Extra hours with no clear purpose are not help.
items: Sessions one to four: the student reframes opinions as knowledge questions unprompted.
Around week six: every claim in the plan has a counterclaim and a specific example.
Teacher comments move from missing knowledge questions to depth and choice of examples.
No tutor can guarantee a TOK grade, and no honest tutor will promise one.

contentBlocks.heading: Starting TOK sessions at home or online in Gurgaon: what to prepare
contentBlocks.body:
Before the first session, gather what the school has already given your child: the TOK task sheet, the prescribed titles if they have been released or the list of 35 IA prompts, any object shortlist or draft plan, the teacher's written comments, and the internal deadlines for the exhibition and the essay. Class notes on the two optional themes help as well. None of it needs tidying first.

The first session is mostly listening. The tutor asks your child to explain, in their own words, what TOK is for. Then comes a short real-life situation, often something from ordinary Gurgaon life such as a disputed traffic challan or a cricket decision overturned on review, and the student is asked to find the knowledge question inside it. That tells the tutor more than any report card. By the end, your child should leave with a single task: rewriting their current title or prompt as a knowledge question, or testing one exhibition object against the prompt.

Parents often ask to sit in. For the demo that is reasonable; for regular sessions it rarely helps, because a student argues less freely with a parent in the room. Ask the tutor for a short message after each session instead, covering what was discussed and what the student will do before the next one. If a home tutor will visit in DLF Phase 2, Rosewood City or Sobha City, sort out gate entry and a quiet table before the first visit, not on the evening itself.

IB Gram shortlists; your family decides. If the demo shows the fit is wrong, ask for a different match straight away rather than hoping it improves. With an IB TOK tutor in Gurgaon, as with any tutor, the time to say so is well before the essay deadline, not after it.
items: Bring the TOK task sheet and the released titles or the 35 IA prompts.
Share the teacher's written comments on objects, plans or drafts.
Note internal deadlines for the exhibition and essay before the first call.

faqs.question: What if the TOK tutor is not working out?

faqs.question: It has been a month and my son's TOK essay plan has not improved. Is that normal?
faqs.answer: No, after a month you should see some change, even if the essay is far from finished. At the least, he should be framing knowledge questions without prompting and naming counterclaims to his own claims. If neither is happening, check whether he does the thinking between sessions and whether the tutor questions or lectures. Raise the concern with the tutor first. If nothing shifts within two or three more sessions, ask IB Gram for a different match.

faqs.question: Can an IB core tutor in Gurgaon handle both TOK and the Extended Essay?
faqs.answer: Yes, some tutors can, although the skills overlap less than families expect. TOK needs someone comfortable arguing across areas of knowledge; the Extended Essay needs a mentor who knows the subject being researched. Because TOK and EE points are combined, one person watching both can spot when one task is starving the other of time. If the EE subject is outside the TOK tutor's strengths, a separate EE mentor is safer, and IB Gram can shortlist for each need.

faqs.answer: Yes, a little: the tutor should work with the two optional themes your child's class studies, not the cousin's. Classes studying different themes will have discussed different examples, and a tutor who ignores that makes sessions feel disconnected from school. contentBlocks.heading: How does IB Gram find the right EE mentor in Gurgaon?
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram matches an Extended Essay request by the subject the essay is written in, how far the student has got and the school's internal deadlines, and then by location and schedule. You send a query or book a free consultation, we shortlist mentors with verified profiles whose subject background fits, and a demo session can be arranged before you commit.

Subject fit matters more here than in ordinary tuition. An economics essay needs a mentor comfortable with secondary data, elasticity and a diagram that carries an argument. A Biology essay needs someone who can spot, in the first conversation, a method that will never produce enough reliable readings. Interdisciplinary essays need a mentor who can hold both subjects without letting one swallow the other. A general DP tutor with no research background will often give polished feedback on the wrong problem, so the first call is mostly questions: which subject, whether a supervisor has been assigned, whether a question exists yet, and what the school's handbook says about outside help. Mention anything that has already gone wrong, such as a question the supervisor rejected, because it changes who is suitable.

Timing shapes the shortlist too. A DP1 student still exploring topics can begin with a session every fortnight. A DP2 student three weeks from the internal draft deadline needs a mentor with evening slots now, and what is possible at that point depends on tutor availability. When you choose an IB Extended Essay tutor in Gurgaon, location usually matters less than subject fit, because most of the work happens in a shared document, but it still decides whether home tuition in your sector is practical.

If the fit is wrong after a few sessions, ask for a different match. It happens. Switching in DP1 is far better than limping through the summer with a mentor the student quietly avoids.

2. We ask where the essay stands: topic, draft question, sources, supervisor comments and schedule.

contentBlocks.heading: Where the Extended Essay sits in the IB Diploma core
contentBlocks.body:
The Extended Essay is an independent research essay of up to 4,000 words, written in one DP subject or as an interdisciplinary essay and supervised by a teacher at the student's own school. It takes roughly 40 hours of work, reflection sessions are recorded along the way, and the essay is graded A to E.

That grade does not stand alone. It combines with the TOK grade for up to 3 diploma points, and an E in either the EE or TOK is a failing condition. Plenty of families new to the IB core EE in Gurgaon assume it can wait until mocks are over. Check the school's internal deadlines before believing that. Roughly 40 hours sounds generous until it is spread across topic reading, a question that changes twice, drafting and redrafting, all alongside Internal Assessment (IA) deadlines in other subjects.

The school supervisor and an outside mentor do different jobs. The supervisor is the teacher the school assigns: the reflection sessions are part of that supervision, and the supervisor knows the internal deadlines and the school's expectations. An IB EE mentor from outside has no formal role at all. What they add is time: an hour a week to question a weak argument, test a source or sit with a student who has not opened the document in ten days. EE supervisor help is valuable but spread thin, because one teacher may be guiding several students alongside a full teaching load.

So the mentor should never become a second supervisor issuing rival instructions. If the supervisor says the question is too broad, the mentor helps the student narrow it rather than arguing that it is fine, and any real change of direction reaches the supervisor through the student. The EE guide was updated for first assessment in 2027, so follow the version your DP coordinator issues and ignore criterion breakdowns or marking advice forwarded from older cohorts.
items: Up to 4,000 words and roughly 40 hours of work, graded A to E.
Supervised by a teacher at the student's school, with recorded reflection sessions.
EE and TOK combine for up to 3 points; an E in either is a failing condition.
Guide updated for first assessment in 2027: use the coordinator's version, not old handouts.

contentBlocks.heading: What do science, economics and English Extended Essays expect?
contentBlocks.body:
Each subject expects research done its own way. In the sciences, the essay needs a focused question and a method that yields enough reliable data to analyse. Economics asks for theory applied to a narrow, real issue and tested with evidence. An English essay builds an argument from close reading of a text. Check the subject guidance in the version of the EE guide your coordinator issues.

Requests for IB Biology EE help often start with a textbook chapter posing as a question, such as how exercise affects the heart. The essay improves once the question is measurable and bounded: the effect of temperature on the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction, over a range the school lab can control. Early on, the mentor asks whether each trial can be repeated enough times and whether lab time will clash with IA practicals. And an EE is not an overgrown lab report; it still needs a discussion that weighs the data and admits what the method could not show.

IB Economics EE help usually starts by shrinking the place and the period. 'Inflation in India' is a book. The price of tomatoes in one wholesale market across a single season of supply shocks is closer to an essay, provided the student can find or collect the data. Theory has to do work rather than decorate: a diagram that carries the argument, figures that test it, and an evaluation that admits what the evidence cannot prove.

English essays are argued, not summarised. A student who loves a novel often proposes a theme, identity in The God of Small Things, say, which could fill a shelf. A narrower question looks at one technique in one text: how Arundhati Roy's movement between the twins' childhood and their adult return controls what the reader is allowed to know. Criticism can support that reading but cannot replace it.
items: Sciences: a measurable, bounded question and a method the school lab can repeat.
Economics: theory applied to one market, place and period, then tested with data.
English: an arguable claim about technique in a text, never a theme summary.
Interdisciplinary: both subjects must do real work; confirm expectations with the supervisor.
